Agentic chat: pesu standalone, kolu for the takeover

Features·seedling·proposed·JUL 25, 2026

pesu is a Buzz-shaped daemon — XS webhook in, an embedded ACP client driving a headless agent it spawns as its own child, replies back in the thread. kolu is not its skeleton but its complement: the takeover surface, where a terminal in the thread's worktree plus claude --resume opens the bot's own conversation.

pesu stands alone; kolu stands beside it. DM the bot in Xyne Spaces and a single daemon does the whole loop: verified webhook in, an ACP session/prompt to a headless agent it spawns as its own child over stdio, the reply posted back to the thread. No proxy process, no socket, no tile in the runtime path — the shape buzz runs in production.Grounded 2026-07-25 by reading the buzz source, not its docs: buzz-acp is simultaneously chat consumer, ACP client, process supervisor, and session pool; it owns each adapter’s stdin/stdout directly (crates/buzz-acp/src/acp.rs) and re-serves ACP on nothing — its observer module advertises publishing telemetry “without exposing a local HTTP port” (crates/buzz-acp/src/observer.rs).

What kolu contributes is deliberately outside that loop: the takeover. The agent’s work is real files in a real git worktree, and its conversation is an ordinary session in the CLI’s own store — so when chat stops being enough, you open a kolu terminal in that worktree, run claude --resume <session-id>, and you are inside the bot’s own conversation: interactive, full history, all its file state around you. pesu does not depend on kolu; kolu completes it.

The shape — one daemon, Buzz-grounded

Component Process Job
Xyne Spaces XS cloud Threads, identity, @mention/DM webhooks, flow cards
pesu standalone daemon (packages/pesu) Chat-frontend plugin (XS first) + author gate + binds; embedded ACP client + adapter supervision; per-thread worktrees
ACP adapter child of pesu The headless agent behind standard ACP — claude-agent-acp, codex-acp; any stdio ACP agent works
kolu separate product, same box The takeover surface — not in the runtime path at all

Xyne Spaces is the first chat frontend, not the design. The chat side of pesu is one thin seam — deliver an inbound message; post, update, and progress a reply — and XS is its first plugin. A Discord-shaped second frontend is architecturally possible from the get-go, because everything past that seam (worktrees, the ACP client, supervision, the takeover ack) never sees XS. One frontend ships in v1; the seam is the commitment, not a second integration.

ACP is still the only protocol on the wire — NDJSON JSON-RPC over the child’s stdio, exactly as the spec ships it — and driving the agent through it deletes the whole observation problem the PTY path had: no bracketed-paste races, no screen-settle detection, no turn-end heuristics. session/prompt returns when the turn ends, and everything in between is a typed frame.Buzz’s production scar tissue stays our checklist: some agents keep streaming after session/cancel, so cancel gets a grace window then a respawn; an in-flight permission request must be answered cancelled before cancelling the turn or the agent deadlocks; the adapter is spawned as a process-group leader and killed as a group so its tool children are reaped. Buzz’s numbers for the same choices: five-second cancel grace, respawn backoff 1s→30s with jitter, a 3-crashes-in-60s circuit breaker (crates/buzz-acp/src/lib.rs, pool.rs).

Session visibility is a log, and is priced like one: pesu appends every ACP frame to a per-session log file beside its bind state. The thread is the product view; the log file is the gore view for debugging. There is no viewer process, because a viewer is not worth a process.An earlier revision of this note ran the adapter behind an acp-proxy in a kolu tile — “chat threads as terminals” — with the tile as the observability story. It shipped as #1985, then was closed unmerged: with a headless adapter the tile can never be more than a read-only rendering of the same session/update stream pesu already consumes — a log viewer — and a log file is the same thing at a fraction of the machinery. (Buzz reached the same verdict from the other direction: rather than any local viewer it encrypts frames onto its own relay and renders them in its chat app — the chat surface is the viewer, which for us is the XS thread itself.) The supervision core and the real-process test harness built in #1985 port into pesu as part of PS1; the socket shape may yet return as the remote-host arm when remote boxes arrive — a distant-future item, not designed here.

Where this deliberately differs from buzz, recorded so the choices are conscious: buzz pools adapter processes and multiplexes sessions across them with preferred, not absolute affinity — a busy pool can silently start a fresh session for a channel, forking its history (crates/buzz-acp/src/pool.rs) — and its replies are not the turn’s output at all: the model is instructed to post by running a buzz messages send CLI. pesu keeps one adapter process per thread and posts the turn’s own result; both simplifications fall out of not pooling.

The takeover — what kolu distinctly adds

The handoff medium is the filesystem plus the session store — no protocol, no export step, no transcript plumbing:

  • Every thread binds to a git worktree. The agent’s tools act on real files; its work is diffable, testable, committable the moment it lands.
  • The conversation is an ordinary CLI session. claude-agent-acp is built on the same engine as the claude CLI, writes a standard JSONL transcript into ~/.claude/projects/, and implements ACP session/load by passing the ACP session id straight into the engine’s resume — the ACP session id is the CLI session id.Facts from the shipped adapter and this dev box, 2026-07-25: claude-agent-acp depends on @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk (it even resolves the bundled claude binary at startup), and its session/load/resumeSession pass params.sessionId as the SDK’s resume option (dist/acp-agent.js). The #1985 smoke sessions sit in ~/.claude/projects/…-packages-acp/*.jsonl as ordinary Claude Code transcripts. codex-acp structurally matches: it advertises loadSession: true and maps the ACP session id onto Codex’s native threadId — the id codex resume takes — read from its shipped bundle but not yet exercised end-to-end, so PS1 proves it once before the ack claims it for codex threads.
  • So the takeover is two commands, not a feature: open a terminal in the worktree; claude --resume <session-id>. pesu’s ack posts both, verbatim.

Not only code. A thread can just as well bind to a knowledge repo:

The agent participates in a discussion among humans, grounded in the repo’s notes, and captures the outcome as markdown commits. The takeover is identical — a terminal and a git repo — because the mechanics never cared what the files were. Repo selection is deliberately dumb: the first message may name an alias from pesu’s configured allowlist (exact token match, no parsing cleverness); no match means the configured default repo.

Decisions

Decision Choice
Library TypeScript, @agentclientprotocol/sdk on its current agent()/client() model — the deprecated connection classes from the #1985 branch never reach master (supersedes #1989)
Package boundary None in v1 — KISS. The ACP client and supervision are pesu modules, ported with their tests from the closed #1985 branch; extract a package only when a second consumer actually exists
Adapter pesu config — any stdio ACP agent; day one claude-agent-acp and codex-acp, pinned as npm deps (no global installs)
Workspace per-thread git worktree, cut from a repo on pesu’s env-configured allowlist (alias → path); first message may name an allowlisted alias verbatim; no match → default repo
Bind state threadId → { cwd, acpSessionId, authorUserId, agent }, JSON file beside pesu
Session visibility every ACP frame appended to a per-session log file beside the bind state; no viewer process
Takeover ack the ack carries the worktree path, the session id, and the exact claude --resume line
Permissions Auto-approved, documented. pesu always answers session/request_permission with the allow_once option, and the bot’s docs state so plainly; interactive approve-from-thread is a Later item, gated on verifying XS flow cards can deliver an app’s button callbacks at all
Reply shape Post once, then updateMessage ≤1/s as the growing reply; split at XS’s 40,000-char capThe XS app API has no delta primitive: updateMessage is a full-body replace, and agentProgress is ephemeral — a Redis-backed working/done pill with a one-line toolLabel, never persisted. The ≤1/s cadence is manners, not a platform limit.

PS1 — the XS round trip + the takeover ack

PS1· webhook → worktree → prompt → reply · ack carries the resume line▶ do next

The user-facing feature is the whole loop: DM the bot, watch the reply land, own the takeover line. Under it rides the one internal port: the supervision core from the closed #1985 branch — process-group spawn and kill, paced respawn, graced cancel, bounded handshake — plus its fake-adapter fixtures and real-process vitest suite, moved into pesu as modules and rebuilt on the SDK’s agent()/client() handler model, so the deprecated connection classes and their biome.jsonc suppression never reach master. The four lifetime bugs review caught on that branch are pinned by those tests; that insurance is the most valuable artifact it produced. acp-proxy, acp-chat, the unix socket, and the PTY rendering are not ported.

pesu: signed webhook (APP_MENTIONED / DIRECT_MESSAGE) → allowlist gate → bind the thread → cut the worktree → spawn the adapter → session/prompt → post the reply. The XS leaf — webhook.ts + HMAC tests, xyneApi.ts + fake-XS tests, fail-fast env config, logging, allowlist, nix run .#pesu — ports from #1810.

The ack is where the takeover lands: worktree path, session id, and the literal claude --resume <id> line. For codex threads the ack includes a resume line only after the threadId mapping is verified against the real codex CLI once (see the takeover footnote) — an unverified resume line is worse than none.

The thread’s ceremony-free home is a DM (every message is delivered); in a channel each message must @mention the app — the apps platform has no follow-the-thread.Follow-the-thread exists only in XS’s separate bot-catalog system, not for installed apps. Two recorded options if the per-message @mention grates: an XS-side feature request, or a pesu-side poller over one dedicated channel’s channelHistory — not built until wanted. pesu answers the webhook 200 immediately and works async — delivery is fire-and-forget, so a slow handler loses events. Deployment shape: systemd user service on 127.0.0.1, fronted by Tailscale Funnel for the stable public webhook URL; secrets reach it only as environment variables — never the repo, logs, or an agent transcript.

Test flows (this PR):

  1. DM the bot a question — the ack arrives with the worktree path and resume line; the reply lands in the thread.
  2. Send a follow-up in the same DM — no new session; the same conversation answers with the earlier context.
  3. Run the ack’s claude --resume line in a terminal in that worktree — the bot’s conversation opens interactively with full history (captured once as PR evidence).
  4. Have someone not on the allowlist DM the bot — one-line decline; nothing spawned.
  5. curl the webhook with a bad X-Xyne-Signature — rejected, nothing posted, nothing created (pinned by a test).
  6. In a channel, @kolu <ask> works; a plain message in the same thread without the @mention does nothing (the documented apps-platform gap).
  7. Ask for something gated — the run proceeds without pausing (auto-approved allow_once), exactly as the bot’s docs say it will.

Done when: DM → worktree exists → reply lands; a second message continues the same session; the ack’s resume line provably opens the same conversation; a forged signature is rejected; a non-operator gets a visible decline, never silence; the ported supervision suite is green inside pesu (crash → respawn → next prompt works; hang → cancel → grace → respawn; parameterized by adapter argv with the deliberately different second vendor retained) with zero deprecated SDK imports and zero lint suppressions for them.

PS2 — turn polish

PS2· growing reply · tool labels · resume across restart○ todo
needs ← PS1

The growing reply (updateMessage ≤1/s, cap-aware split); tool_call frames → agentProgress labels while the turn runs; session/load on pesu restart, so the daemon holds no conversation state beyond its bind file.Both pinned adapters advertise loadSession; resume replays the session’s history as the same session/update stream, so pesu’s cursor logic needs no special path. For an adapter that doesn’t advertise it, pesu starts a fresh session and says so in the thread — visibly, never silently.

Test flows (this PR):

  1. A long task — one message grows in place instead of a stream of separate messages.
  2. The progress pill changes labels as the agent moves between tools; it clears when the turn ends.
  3. systemctl --user restart pesu mid-conversation, then send the next DM — the conversation continues with prior context; no earlier reply is double-posted.
  4. Provoke a reply longer than 40,000 chars — it splits into consecutive messages instead of failing.

Done when: restart pesu mid-conversation; the next DM continues the same conversation with prior context, without double-posting earlier replies.

Later, on demand (small bounded additions, not phases): approve from the thread — a session/request_permission becoming a button card in the thread is designed only after verifying the XS apps platform can deliver an app’s button callbacks at all (unconfirmed today; until then documented auto-approve is the contract, and a cancel must resolve any pending request as cancelled first — the buzz deadlock lesson); a second chat frontend (Discord-shaped) behind the same seam; per-thread agent selection UX (the wire already takes any adapter); goose as an optional agent — one config entry, no code.Recorded 2026-07-25 from the adapter and goose sources: goose’s native ACP is strongest on session persistence and cancellable permission requests — advantages that become observable only once resume-across-restart (PS2) and approve-from-thread land — and wins decisively on provider breadth (15+ API/cloud/local model providers), at the cost of one more runtime between the thread and the model when a claude/codex subscription is already the target.

Background

Why chat at all. Anthropic shipped Claude Tag — one shared Claude per channel, pursuing tasks “over hours or days” — and Karpathy called the shape “the 3rd major redesign of LLM UIUX”: the agent as a persistent coworker that lives where the team already works.The proof-point Anthropic leads with is blunt: “65% of our product team’s code is created by our internal version.” The human’s job shifts from driving keystrokes to managing agents. Buzz is the same thesis as a product — chat where agents are coworkers in channels — and XS-plus-pesu is that exact shape on infrastructure you own.

What the moat actually is. The properties that distinguish this from Claude Tag — the shell and files real, the host yours, the model swappable (the adapter is config) — are properties of self-hosting pesu, and they hold with no kolu anywhere in sight.Marc Andreessen, on what agent research converged on: “an agent is … a language model, and above that a bash shell … and then a file system, and the state is stored in files” — and “your agent is now actually independent of the model … you can swap out a different LLM underneath.” That is this architecture, line for line. kolu’s distinct contribution is the takeover: because the agent’s state is files in a worktree and a session in the CLI’s own store, the product where you already live in terminals is one cd and one --resume from continuing the bot’s work by hand. Chat owns the breadth; kolu owns the moment delegation stops being enough.

The XS apps platform, as grounded

The contract PS1 builds against — read from the xyne-spaces source (2026-07-13), not its docs, because XS has three separate integration systems that are easy to conflate: the bot catalog (backend-native bots), incoming webhooks (URL-embedded-secret message drops), and the apps platform — installed apps with a webhook URL, a bearer token, and a signing secret. pesu is an installed app; only the third system applies.

Event Fires when
APP_MENTIONED the app is explicitly @mentioned in a channel — carries conversationId (thread), channelId, messageId, sender userId, body as HTML + plain text, attachments
DIRECT_MESSAGE every message in a 1:1 DM with the app (same shape, no senderName)
USER_MENTIONED a human is @mentioned where the app is present — observer signal

Auth, both directions, one secret. Deliveries carry X-Xyne-Signature — HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the app’s signing secret; no timestamp or replay scheme, so verification is a constant-time compare and replay is an accepted, recorded risk. The bearer token is a JWT signed HS256 with that same secret, no expiry — it lives until regenerated.

The app API (/api/apps, bearer): chat/postMessage (text, markdown, or structured content; conversationId targets a thread) · chat/updateMessage · chat/agentProgress · chat/channelHistory / chat/conversationReplies (catch-up after downtime) · channel/openDm · user/info.No webhook payload carries a sender email (the DM payload omits even the display name) — pesu resolves people through user/info and caches them. Event delivery is fire-and-forget with no retries: a delivery missed while pesu is down is lost; the read APIs recover.

Out of scope

  • Remote boxes — in scope for the product, distant future for this plan. Everything here is one machine: pesu, the adapters, the worktrees, and kolu side by side. When multi-host arrives, the remote arm may well turn out to be a proxy-shaped process re-serving ACP from the far host — noted so the option isn’t forgotten, deferred so it isn’t designed prematurely.
  • kolu changes — none at all: no new session kind, no dock/awareness work, no viewer. The takeover uses plain terminals kolu already has.
  • PTY-agent observation — session watchers and every interactive tile a human drives stay exactly as they are.
  • Bot secrets in a web UI — pesu config is env/systemd beside the daemon.

Done criterion (full tree)

DM the bot → a headless session answers from a per-thread worktree → the reply grows in place → restart pesu and the thread resumes → and at any point, open a terminal in that worktree, run the ack’s claude --resume line, and continue the bot’s own conversation by hand.
